activity.overview: Read a short fact sheet and write a complete argument in one class period.
activity.prompt: Lakeview High School is deciding whether students must lock their phones away for the whole school day. Read the fact sheet, then write an argument that takes a clear position on the proposal (you may support it, oppose it, or propose a precise alternative). Use at least two facts or quotations from the fact sheet, explain how each supports your claim, address the strongest counterclaim, and end with a conclusion that follows from your argument. You have one class period.
activity.subject: english-language-arts
activity.title: On-Demand Argument: Phones in Class

readings.attribution: Written for EducateOS. An illustrative fact sheet; the school and its numbers are invented for teaching.
readings.body:
The proposal
Lakeview High School is considering a rule that students lock their phones in a pouch from the first bell to the last bell. Students would keep the phones; they just could not open the pouches until dismissal.

Facts the committee collected
- In a one-week count, Lakeview teachers recorded an average of 11 phone-related interruptions per class period.
- 64 percent of Lakeview students surveyed said they check their phones during class "often" or "very often."
- 58 percent of parents surveyed said they want to be able to reach their children during the school day, most often to change pickup plans.
- Several schools that adopted pouch rules reported fewer interruptions and fewer conflicts that started online during the day. Researchers caution that those schools changed other things at the same time.
- The pouches would cost about $25 per student, or roughly $30,000 for the school.

Voices from the hearing
A teacher: "I spend the first five minutes of every class getting students to put their phones away. That is five minutes I never get back."
A parent: "When there was a lockdown drill last year, the first thing I wanted was to hear my son's voice."
A student: "Some of us use our phones for translation and for our planners. Treat us like people who can learn to manage them."
A counselor: "The lunchroom is quieter now. I am not sure it is happier."
